query: For high-entropy alloys used in thermal-insulation applications, what testable hypothesis could be made about an unspecified predictive approach for accurately identifying materials with low phonon thermal conductivity? The hypothesis should explain why the approach would work, predict its improvement over current predictions, define its applicability limits, identify supporting evidence, and specify a decisive experimental benchmark and outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A Debye/DFT‐based computational approach that explicitly models lattice distortions and chemical bond fluctuations in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) will predict low lattice thermal conductivity (κL) with approximately 20% lower error relative to conventional empirical models. This approach works because it accounts for the enhanced phonon scattering arising from mass, strain, and bond fluctuations inherent in multi‐element disordered structures.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys with a disordered multi-component structure, exemplified by systems like PbSnTeSe or FeCoCrMnNi, used in thermal insulation or thermoelectric applications.
generation.intervention: Application of a computational predictive framework combining Debye theory and density functional theory (DFT) calculations (with special quasi-random structure models) to calculate phonon dispersion and κL across a range of temperatures (e.g., 300–700 K).
generation.conditions: Simulations performed at and above room temperature, where phonon scattering due to lattice distortions is significant. The model is applied to HEAs that conform to typical high-entropy alloy formation rules (i.e. multiple principal elements with moderate to high atomic size mismatch).
generation.structural_mediator: The intrinsic lattice distortions and chemical bond fluctuations (including variations in force-constants from mass and electronegativity differences) that enhance phonon scattering in the alloy’s crystal lattice.
generation.mechanism: By explicitly incorporating the effects of mass, strain, and chemical bond fluctuations into Debye/DFT models, the approach captures the reduction in phonon velocities and enhanced scattering events that lower κL. This leads to predictions more aligned with experimental thermal conductivities observed in low-κL HEAs.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will predict κL values that closely match experimental measurements (e.g., near 0.4 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ at 300 K for some thermoelectric HEAs) with an estimated improvement of around 20% in prediction accuracy over simpler empirical or semi-analytical models. In addition, the predicted trend of decreasing κL with increasing temperature due to enhanced phonon scattering will be reproduced.
generation.baseline: Baseline predictions based on conventional empirical rules or simplified analytical models that do not account in full for the disorder-induced phonon scattering effects in HEAs.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to be applicable primarily to HEAs with moderate atomic size and electronegativity differences. It may not perform well for alloys with extreme local bonding variations or where electronic contributions dominate the thermal conductivity, as well as in cases where anharmonic effects are too large to be well captured by Debye/DFT approximations.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement (e.g., exactly 20% lower error) is uncertain due to potential system-specific anharmonicities and limitations in capturing very low-q phonon behavior. Additionally, deviations may arise in HEAs with unusually strong chemical bond fluctuations or non-standard microstructural features not fully represented in standard SQS models.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a set of well-characterized high-entropy alloys with available experimental κL data across a temperature range (e.g., 300–700 K). Apply the Debye/DFT predictive approach to compute the lattice thermal conductivity for these alloys using SQS models. Compare the computationally predicted κL values with experimental measurements obtained via techniques such as time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) or the Green–Kubo method in controlled laboratory setups.
measurements: Lattice thermal conductivity (κL) at multiple temperatures
Phonon dispersion curves to verify predicted scattering trends
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Debye/DFT based predictions deviate from the experimental κL values by significantly more than the estimated 20% improvement relative to conventional models (i.e., errors exceed acceptable error bounds), or if the predicted temperature trends do not match the experimental behavior, then the hypothesis that this approach yields improved predictive accuracy for low κL in HEAs is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The difference in electronegativity (another intrinsic characteristic of element) affects the local chemical bonding and plays a vital role for the properties of high-entropy materials, such as the strength and ductility of high-entropy alloys (, , ) for engineered applications, the charge redistribution of high-entropy catalysts () for hydrogen evolution reaction, and the electron transport of high-entropy oxides () for lithium-ion battery. Similar to the mass and strain field fluctuations, the electronegativity difference could increase the complexity of chemical bonding between atoms as the chemical bond fluctuation. Therefore, the contribution of electronegativity difference was also included into the Callaway-Debye model for lattice thermal conductivity calculation (Supplementary Text and table S6). In conclusion, we have reported the first experimental investigation of the acoustic phonon dispersions in a High-Entropy Alloy, complemented by the GVDOS survey, at room and low temperature. FeCoCrMnNi is a 5-element random alloy, and, despite the inherent disorder, its phonon dynamics closely resemble that of the pure elements composing it and the corresponding binary alloys. More specifically, acoustic phonons disperse throughout the whole Brillouin zone up to energies between 20 and 30 meV, exhibiting an attenuation stronger than in simple elements, but of the same order of magnitude as in binary alloys. The whole attenuation behavior can be understood in terms of scattering from force-constant fluctuations, which have been estimated to amount to ~20% using a simple theoretical model, a value comparable with calculations of Mu and co-authors on binary and ternary alloys made of the same elements. Thermoelectric materials have attracted extensive attention because they can directly convert waste heat into electric energy. As a brand-new method of alloying, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted much attention in the fields of materials science and engineering. Recent researches have found that HEAs could be potentially good thermoelectric (TE) materials. In this study, special quasi-random structures (SQS) of PbSnTeSe high-entropy alloys consisting of 64 atoms have been generated. The thermoelectric transport properties of the highest-entropy PbSnTeSe-optimized structure were investigated by combining calculations from first-principles density-functional theory and on-the-fly machine learning with the semiclassical Boltzmann transport theory and Green–Kubo theory. The results demonstrate that PbSnTeSe HEA has a very low lattice thermal conductivity. The electrical conductivity, thermal electronic conductivity and Seebeck coefficient have been evaluated for both n-type and p-type doping. cited_evidence.text: Using the same approach, the value of κL was computed for various temperatures in the range 300–700 K (Figure 9). At 300 K, the κL value is 0.4 W K−1 m−1, which is a very low value of the lattice thermal conductivity, favorable for thermoelectric materials. This is due to the lattice distortion effect of high-entropy alloys that can reduce phonon velocity and enhance phonon scattering, resulting in low thermal conductivity. Additionally, one can observe that when the temperature rises, the thermal conductivity of the lattice decreases, which is also due to an increase in phonon scattering at higher temperatures.

chosen.approach: Computational prediction of lattice thermal conductivity using Debye/DFT models
